q: Which of these is NOT an object of an MS Access database?
x: Access database objects include tables, queries, forms, reports, macros and modules. A slide belongs to a PowerPoint presentation, not to an Access database.

q: A Fee field stores amounts in rupees and paisa, such as 1250.50, and is used in money calculations. Which Access data type suits it best?
x: Currency is meant for money values and keeps them accurate in calculations. Short Text cannot be added or multiplied as numbers, and AutoNumber is filled in by Access itself.

q: A Remarks field will hold a teacher's comments, often several paragraphs and more than 255 characters long. Which data type should it have?
x: Long Text (Memo) holds long passages of text. Short Text is limited to 255 characters, so longer comments would be cut off.

q: A field stores each school's website address so that clicking the value opens the site in a browser. Which data type is meant for this?
x: A Hyperlink field stores an address that opens when it is clicked. Short Text could store the address as plain characters, but clicking it would not open the site.

q: Which view of an Access table is used to type field names, choose data types and set field properties?
x: Design View shows the table's structure: field names, data types and properties. Datasheet View shows the records in rows and columns for entering data.

q: A Number field will store the population of each district, always a whole number of up to about 5,000,000. Which is the smallest whole-number Field Size that can hold it?
x: Byte holds 0 to 255 and Integer up to 32,767, both far too small; Long Integer holds whole numbers up to about 2 billion. Double is for numbers with fractions, not a whole-number size.

q: Which field property, when set to Yes, stops Access from saving a record while that field is left empty?
x: Required = Yes forces the user to enter a value before the record is saved. Default Value only fills in a starting value, and Caption only changes the label shown for the field.

q: The Marks field has a Validation Rule. Which property holds the message, such as "Marks must be 0 to 100", that Access shows when an entry breaks the rule?
x: Validation Text is the message displayed when the Validation Rule is broken. Input Mask controls the pattern of typing, and Format controls how values are displayed.

q: A field is set as the primary key of an Access table. Which entry will Access refuse in that field?
o: A value typed in capital letters
A value entered through a form
A value already used in another record
A value entered in Datasheet View
x: A primary key must be unique (and not empty), so a value that already exists in another record is refused. How the value is typed or where it is entered does not matter.

q: Customers and Orders are joined one-to-many on CustomerID (a Number field), with referential integrity enforced and "Cascade Update Related Fields" ticked. Customer 7 has four orders. The user changes this customer's CustomerID from 7 to 70. What happens?
o: Access refuses the change because orders exist
The four orders change to CustomerID 70 automatically
The four orders keep CustomerID 7 and lose their link
x: Cascade Update copies a change of the primary key to every matching foreign key, so all four orders now show 70. Without the cascade option, Access would refuse the change while related orders exist.

q: Table Result has the primary key (RollNo, Subject) and holds the records (5, Maths, 70), (5, Physics, 60) and (6, Maths, 80). Which new record will Access refuse?
x: With a composite key only the pair (RollNo, Subject) must be unique, and (6, Maths) already exists. The other records repeat a RollNo or a Subject on its own, which is allowed.

q: A table's ID field is AutoNumber. Records with IDs 1 to 5 were added, and then the record with ID 5 was deleted. The database has not been compacted. What ID does the next new record get?
x: AutoNumber keeps counting from the last number it gave out and does not reuse a deleted number, so the next record gets 6. AutoNumber values are never typed by the user.

q: Which type of Access query raises the Price of every Physics book by 10% in one step?
x: An update query changes the values in many existing records at once. A select query only shows records, and an append query adds records to another table.

q: Which kind of Access query only shows the records that meet its criteria and never changes the data in the tables?
x: A select query retrieves and displays data. Update, delete and make-table queries are action queries that change data or create tables.

q: In the Access query design grid, in which row is a condition such as >500 typed so that only matching records are shown?
x: Conditions go in the Criteria row under the field they test. The Sort row sets the order, the Show box decides whether the field appears, and the Field row names the field.

q: Which Access action query copies the records it selects into a brand-new table?
x: A make-table query creates a new table from the query's result. An append query adds the selected records to a table that already exists.

q: Which Access query shows summarised values in a grid, with the values of one field as row headings and the values of another field as column headings?
x: A crosstab query summarises data (for example sums or counts) in a row-and-column layout like a spreadsheet. A parameter query asks the user for a value when it runs.

q: In an Access query, the criteria under City is `[Enter city name]`. What happens when the query is run?
o: Access asks the user to type a city and shows the records for it
Access shows the records whose City is the text Enter city name
Access shows an error because of the square brackets
Access deletes the records that have an empty City
x: Text in square brackets that is not a field name makes a parameter query: Access shows the text as a prompt and uses the typed value as the criteria. It would be literal text only if typed in quotes.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
What does this query return?
```
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Book WHERE Subject = 'Maths' AND Price > 450;
```
x: The Maths books cost 450, 700 and 400; only 700 is greater than 450, so the count is 1. Algebra at 450 is not counted because > does not include 450.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
What does this query return?
```
SELECT Title FROM Book WHERE NOT Subject = 'Maths' ORDER BY Price DESC;
```
x: The books that are not Maths are Optics 600, Atoms 350 and Mechanics 500; DESC sorts from the highest price, giving Optics, Mechanics, Atoms. Atoms first would be ascending order.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In Access, the criteria `Between 400 And 600` is typed under Price. How many records does the query return?
x: Between includes both end values, so 450, 600, 500 and 400 match: 4 records. Only 700 and 350 are outside the range; leaving out the two end values would give 2.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In an empty column of the query's Field row, `NewPrice: [Price]+50` is typed. When the query runs, what is shown for Optics, and what happens to the Book table?
o: 650 is shown; the table's Price becomes 650
600 is shown; a NewPrice column is added to the table
650 is shown; the table's Price stays 600
An error is shown because NewPrice is not a field
x: A calculated field in a select query is worked out each time the query runs (600 + 50 = 650) and is not stored. Only an update query would change the Price in the table.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In the design grid, "Maths" is typed under Subject and <500 under Price, both in the same Criteria row. Which titles are returned?
x: Criteria in the same row are joined with AND, so a book must be Maths and cost under 500: Algebra 450 and Geometry 400. Reading them as OR would add Calculus and Atoms.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
How many rows does this query return?
```
SELECT DISTINCT Subject FROM Book;
```
x: DISTINCT removes repeated values, leaving Maths, Physics and Chemistry: 3 rows. Without DISTINCT one row per book, 6 rows, would be shown.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In Access, the criteria `Like "*o*"` is typed under Title. Which titles are returned?
x: *o* matches any title that contains the letter o anywhere: Optics, Atoms and Geometry. Access's Like ignores letter case, so the capital O of Optics matches too; Mechanics has no o.

q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
What does this query return?
```
SELECT Title FROM Book
WHERE Subject = 'Physics' OR Subject = 'Maths' AND Price > 500
ORDER BY BookID;
```
x: AND is applied before OR, so the condition is Physics OR (Maths AND Price > 500): Optics and Mechanics, plus Calculus at 700, in BookID order 2, 3, 5. Applying OR first would give only Optics and Calculus.

q: Which form control shows the value of a field and lets the user type or change it?
x: A bound text box displays a field's value and accepts typing. A label only shows fixed text, such as a heading or a field's caption.

q: Which view shows how a report will look on paper, page by page, before it is printed?
x: Print Preview shows the finished pages as they will print. Design View shows the sections and controls for editing the layout, not the final pages.

q: What is the main purpose of a form in Access?
o: To enter, view and edit data in a convenient layout
To print grouped totals on paper
To define the data types of fields
x: A form is a screen for working with records comfortably. The data itself is stored in tables, printed summaries are made with reports, and data types are set in table Design View.

q: Where does the Form Header section appear when a form is opened in Form view?
o: Once at the top of the form, whichever record is shown
Above every record shown on the form
Only when the last record is shown
At the bottom of every printed page
x: The Form Header is shown once at the top of the form and does not change from record to record, so it suits titles and logos. Data for each record appears in the Detail section.

q: A report on Student(Name, City) is grouped by City. There are 3 students from Lahore, 2 from Karachi and 1 from Multan. How many times is the City Header section printed?
x: A group header is printed once at the start of each group, and there are 3 cities, so it prints 3 times. Printing once per student, 6 times, is what the Detail section does.

q: A school logo must appear at the top of a form and stay the same for every record. Which control is used for it?
x: An image control shows a fixed picture that does not depend on the record. A bound object frame shows a picture stored in a field of each record, so it changes from record to record.

q: On a form, a text box bound to RollNo has an attached label that shows "RollNo". To make the label show "Roll Number", which property is changed?
o: The Control Source of the text box
The Record Source of the form
The Default Value of the text box
x: A label's text is its Caption property. Changing the text box's Control Source would change which field it shows, not the words beside it.

q: A form's Allow Additions property is set to No. What can a user no longer do through this form?
x: Allow Additions controls only whether new records can be added. Editing existing records is controlled by the separate Allow Edits property.

q: On a form, a text box has the Control Source `=[Qty]*[Price]`. The user clicks in it and tries to type 500. What happens?
o: 500 replaces the result and is saved in the table
500 is saved into the Price field
Access does not allow it, because the control shows a calculated expression
Qty is changed so that the result becomes 500
x: A calculated control is bound to an expression, not a field, so it cannot be edited; Access says the control is bound to the expression. Its value is never written to the table.

q: A report on Student(Name, City) is grouped by City in ascending order and sorted by Name within each group. The records are (Sana, Multan), (Ali, Lahore), (Zain, Karachi), (Bilal, Karachi), (Hina, Lahore). In which order are the names printed?
x: Cities in ascending order are Karachi, Lahore, Multan, and names are sorted inside each: Bilal, Zain, then Ali, Hina, then Sana. Sorting by name alone, ignoring the groups, would give Ali first.
